name: Particle Field Hero
summary: A dense GPU point-cloud forms a loose constellation that idles on slow brownian drift and physically reacts to the cursor — particles scatter under pointer proximity and spring back to cohesion. Emergent connective lines between neighbors read as a living network without any literal iconography.

composition: Split emphasis: a stacked condensed headline + stats + CTA column on one side, the particle cluster on the other; or the field envelops centered type as ambient dust.
The cluster has a shape — a loose sphere/nebula with a dense core and sparse ember edges; a uniform full-screen scatter reads as noise, not an object.
Type stays static and authoritative; the energy budget is spent entirely in the field.
layering: The field is a discrete depth plane behind the text plane; text never loses legibility to particles.
Connective lines are emergent — drawn between nearby particles as a byproduct of position, never keyframed — so the network feels alive.
Dark/light sibling variants share one engine: invert the ground, keep the accent identical.
lighting: Additive-glow: particles are self-luminous with soft bloom, brightest at the cluster core, falling off at edges.
On dark grounds the points read as light emission; on light grounds the same points read as confetti/dust — the ground flips the metaphor for free.
typography: Condensed bold grotesque headline, tightly stacked 2-3 lines; a single underlined/gradient accent word for emphasis.
Small clean stats/caption row grounds the spectacle in facts.

rules: Pick ONE gradient duo (e.g. hot-to-cool) and let it be the entire color story: particles, connective lines, and the type accent all share it.
Dark/light variants change only the ground color, never the accent — proving the system is an engine, not a composition.

easing: Idle: perpetual low-amplitude brownian float with slow global rotation — the cluster breathes, never rests.
Interaction: quick repulsion (~200-400ms) followed by a springy elastic return to each particle's cohesion target.
pacing: Two timescales at once: slow luxurious global drift + fast local pointer reactions — the contrast is the delight.
Disturbances re-cohere within a second or two so the object never stays broken.
choreography: Two motion layers: (1) whole-cluster rotation/float, (2) per-particle repulsion by pointer distance; lines form and break as a consequence.
Sweeping the cursor carves a readable wake through the cluster — input velocity maps to disturbance size.

whenToUse: AI/network/data products where 'connecting the dots' is the literal metaphor.
Dark-stage tech heroes needing GPU craft with tiny asset weight (no imagery required).
When a brief needs matching dark/light theme variants from one system.
whenNotToUse: Brands wanting warmth/humanity or print-editorial calm — the field reads clinical.
Low-end devices: thousands of animated particles with per-frame neighbor-line computation cause jank; needs a static fallback.
AI-marketing contexts where the pattern is saturated — the family risks cliche precisely because it works; rotate against alternatives.

notes: One full-frame GPU field per surface — never stack with fluid or glitch.
The W9 forge hero (140k-particle TSL compute galaxy) is our in-house demonstration of this family's core mechanic.

antiRepetition.notes: Same cluster as gpu-fluid-overlay and hover-morph-distortion.

sources.title: AI Particle Cluster Hero
sources.motionEvidence: Founder monitor session, live demo: idle drift observed over time; cursor swept through the cluster at varied speeds — repulsion, wake carving, and elastic re-cohesion captured across interaction states; dark and light sibling slides both driven.

exemplars.promptSummary: Thousands of fine points converging into a soft luminous nucleus with link-lines, single cyan-to-violet gradient on deep space black — emergent-order particle field.
exemplars.notes: ORIGINAL render (Replicate black-forest-labs/flux-2-pro, ~$0.06). Subject deliberately distinct from any analyzed source template. Illustrates the family aesthetic target (palette/composition/lighting); does NOT demonstrate runtime motion or in-engine execution.
